source_document.body:
PARIS — France kicked off an initiative with its defense industry to produce counter-drone systems, a new chapter in efforts to foster a local drone ecosystem through “pacts” with industry that bring together firms and military end users, cut procurement red tape and focus on fast contract delivery.
The new pact adds a counter-drone dimension to France’s existing drone pact and will run to the end of summer 2027, said Emmanuel Levacher, chairman of defense-industry association Gicat and the CEO of military vehicle maker Arquus.
“We then hope it will be renewed while incorporating both drone and counter-drone, the idea being that one does not go without the other,” Levacher told Defense News on Wednesday night, after a presentation of the new counter-drone pact in the offices of semiconductor maker STMicroelectronics, just outside Paris.
The drone pact announced in June 2024 has been an attempt by France to play catch up in tactical drones and loitering munitions, led by the country’s Directorate General for Armament together with Gicat. Following up on the success of the original drone pact, France in November announced a similar pact for naval drones , on the occasion of the Euronaval defense trade show.
The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have been a “quite brutal reality check,” and French forces have an urgent need for counter-drone capabilities, Alice Rufo, France’s junior minister for the armed forces, said in a speech at the presentation. She said France has already faced problems related to having insufficient counter-drone capability, without providing details.
France has faced multiple incidents with drones overflying sensitive military sites, including the Île Longue nuclear submarine base in December 2025 and the Toulon naval base in October this year. French media have also reported drones flying over a Eurenco explosives plant in Bergerac and a freight train carrying Leclerc main battle tanks near Mulhouse in November 2025.
The new pact covers systems to counter unmanned aerial vehicles but also maritime and ground drones, according to Levacher. The Gicat chairman said he expects most or all of the 200 partners in the drone pact to participate in the counter-drone initiative.
The goal of the counter-drone pact is “to really be in contact with the armed forces” to understand their requirements, as well as with the DGA to facilitate testing, validation and orders, Levacher said.
“The idea is really to bring together all the stakeholders to create this cross-pollination, speed, contacts,” Levacher said. “This pact is a way of saying that this is an area that does still need to structure and organize itself a little.”
The drone pact has functioned as a meeting place for industry where companies have been able to find project partners, as well as a forum to share feedback from Ukraine, according to Levacher. The DGA uses the drone pact as a framework for informal calls for ideas.
While the demand, the connections and the ecosystem are primarily French, the drone pact firms also pursue export opportunities, Levacher said.
Within the framework of the drone pact, French startup Harmattan AI won a contract in June 2025 to supply the French Army with 1,000 low-cost drones, which it delivered in January this year ahead of the Orion exercise.
